nodes.text: We say that “voltage drops” across a resistor.
The current is the same at A and B!
The current is lower through this whole circuit due to the resistor.

nodes.detailed_figure_description: A closed circuit is drawn as a loop crowded with small rectangular blocks labeled e⁻, representing electrons. At the top of the loop, the blocks pass through a zigzag resistor labeled R, illustrating a traffic-jam mental model. A battery at the bottom is labeled V, with a magenta plus sign on the left and a blue minus sign on the right.
nodes.figure_alternative: Traffic-jam model of electrons crowded around a closed circuit containing resistor R and voltage source V.

nodes.text: A flashlight bulb draws 300 mA from its 1.5 V battery. What’s the resistance of the bulb? If the battery degrades and only produces 1.2 V how would the current change?

nodes.figure_alternative: Drawing of a lit flashlight with a bulb and two batteries inside its casing.

nodes.spoken_math_alternative: Current equals voltage divided by resistance. Therefore, resistance equals voltage divided by current, which equals 1.5 volts divided by 0.30 amperes, or 5.0 ohms.
When the voltage changes to 1.2 volts, current equals 1.2 volts divided by 5.0 ohms, which is 0.24 amperes, or 240 milliamperes.
